newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian refinery under scrutiny for excess capacity.
newsitem.headline: Indian refinery under scrutiny for excess capacity.

text.p: India has ordered a cost audit of Mangalore Refineries and Petrochemicals Ltd (MRPL) after finding it has more than its sanctioned refining capacity, a Petroleum Ministry official said on Wednesday.

"The cost audit committee will comprise senior officials from the Petroleum Ministry. Its report will work out the actual refining capacity based on which the refining margin will be assessed," the official, who asked not to be named, said.
India has an administered pricing policy for petroleum products. Oil refineries receive operating costs and a 12 percent return on net worth annually from the Petroleum Ministry.

The full 12 percent is paid only if a refinery achieves its target. If a refinery has invested in more than the capacity it has received clearance for, then its net worth is higher, and the Petroleum Ministry annual payout increases.

Last year the Petroleum Ministry appointed a committee to examine the 132 percent cost over-run incurred by MRPL in setting up its 3.0 million tonne refinery at Mangalore in the south Indian state of Karnataka.

The refinery, promoted jointly by state-run Hindustan Petroleum Corp Ltd and Indian Rayon & Industries Ltd, was approved by the Indian government at a cost of 11.60 billion rupees ($325 million) in April 1991.
The refinery was completed in March 1996 at a cost of 26.97 billion rupees.
In its report, the committee said: "There was a change in scope of the project which contributed to the increase in cost estimates."
"The crude distillation unit, hydrocracker and visbreaker unit at the refinery were designed for a capacity greater than 3.7 million tonne instead of the licensed 3.0 million," the committee said.
"The additional cost of designing higher capacities in the refinery has been estimated at 2.0 billion rupees," the committee added.

Based on the committee's report, the Petroleum Ministry has asked HPCL's chairman H.L. Zutshi to explain the reasons for designing excess capacity, for which the Ministry has not given any prior approval, the official said.
